title: The diabolical defending of Manchester City
gist: Lawyer DAT Green analyses a Premier League disciplinary commission's 40-page decision finding Manchester City deliberately concealed its finances through sham contracts involving more than £800m across 2009-10 to 2017-18 and obstructed the investigation. He argues the ruling looks appeal-proof, sanctions will be onerous, and the club's aggressive litigation strategy has made its position worse.

themes.theme: Premier League findings against Manchester City

insights.claim: A Premier League-appointed disciplinary commission found Manchester City seriously breached the league's financial rules, devising a scheme with sham contracts to deliberately conceal its true financial position, and failed to cooperate with the investigation.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Major governance and regulatory finding against one of Europe's most valuable football clubs, with implications for its owners, sponsors and the league's competitive integrity.
insights.quote: Manchester City devised an overall scheme and also various methods to deliberately conceal and disguise its true financial position from the league

insights.claim: The wrongdoing spanned seasons 2009-10 to 2017-18 and involved more than £800m, a sustained and systemic exercise from which City benefited by outspending rivals and dominating English football.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Scale of the sums and duration point toward severe sanctions, potentially affecting club valuation and commercial revenues.
insights.quote: It was a sustained, substantial and systemic exercise.

insights.claim: Only a redacted 40-page summary was published; the evidence, factual findings and legal rulings sit in unpublished appendices, so conclusions must for now be taken at face value.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Full details may yet emerge and move perceptions further.

insights.claim: The decision looks fairly appeal-proof because the commission found that even absent wrongful intent many breaches would still stand as non-compliance, so City must overturn both culpability findings and factual findings.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Low probability of the club escaping liability via appeal.
insights.quote: The disciplinary commission’s decision is not only damning, but it looks fairly appeal-proof.
insights.locator: The disciplinary commission’s decision is not

insights.claim: The commission took nearly two years and built dedicated evidential appendices for each charge, making an appellate attack an immense task; a further High Court challenge on law or procedure has only a remote chance of success.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Litigation may drag on but outcome risk skews against the club.
insights.locator: The commission has taken a long time

insights.claim: City appeared to have until 2 October to appeal and an appeal would not be surprising; Green suggests the club would be more sensible to focus on the coming sanctions hearing, where onerous penalties are expected.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Watch the sanctions hearing as the key catalyst for practical consequences.
insights.locator: There will be a further hearing

insights.claim: The commission found City made 'concerted efforts to stop and frustrate' the investigation; the resulting non-cooperation charges, nearly all proved, will make appeals harder and inform tougher sanctions.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Combative governance culture increases downside in regulatory disputes.
insights.locator: The decision of the disciplinary commission

insights.claim: The decision states several City witnesses were 'dishonest' and gave evidence they knew to be untrue, putting the club at a disadvantage across the litigation.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Credibility findings weigh heavily in sanctions and any appeal.
insights.quote: The witnesses gave evidence “which they knew to be untrue”.
insights.locator: Here, there is also the problem

insights.claim: City's approach mirrors its earlier stance toward Uefa: the chairman reportedly preferred to spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyers to sue Uefa for a decade rather than accept a fine, and an internal message said Uefa responds only to aggression.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: A pattern of litigation-as-strategy that may not translate to the Premier League's disciplinary structure.
insights.quote: “Uefa doesn't respond to anything other than aggression”
insights.locator: What can explain such an aggressive

insights.claim: Green argues money spent on lawyers is of no avail when facts and law are against you, and that City's strategy was 'diabolical' in the literal sense — pursued knowing it would likely fail and make things harder, perhaps hoping to push the league into settlement.
insights.speaker: DAT Green
insights.so_what: Settlement hopes should be discounted; the club has 'scored own goals' in the litigation.
insights.quote: Law is not magic, and lawyers are not magicians.
